# Operating system and time-sharing (Unix) (`operating_system_time_sharing`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: needs programmable_computer, computer_memory; helped by programming_languages_compilers
- Core idea: An operating system is the program that is always running and manages the machine for all other programs: it starts and stops them, shares out memory, and hides the details of discs, tapes and terminals. By switching the processor among programs many times a second it lets dozens of people use one computer at once from typewriter terminals, each as if alone, and it keeps them from damaging each other's work. The Unix design keeps this simple: ordinary files are sequences of bytes in a tree of named directories; devices are treated as files; programs are small tools that each do one job and can be joined so that the output of one feeds the next; and the system is written in a high-level language so that it can be moved to new machines.
- Pitfalls:
  - Running one job at a time while an expensive machine waits for a human or a card reader
  - Building one huge system that tries to do everything; Multics was years late, and Unix began as the reaction to it
  - No protection between users and the system, so that one faulty program stops the machine for everyone
  - Writing the system in the machine language of one computer, so that it dies with that model
- History: europe: 1959 – Strachey's paper on time-sharing in large computers; 1962 Atlas supervisor with virtual memory (Manchester); americas: 1956 – GM-NAA I/O batch monitor for the IBM 704; 1961 CTSS time-sharing system (Corbató, MIT); 1964–1969 Multics (MIT, General Electric, Bell Labs); 1969 Unix (Thompson and Ritchie, Bell Labs), rewritten in C in 1973, described publicly in 1974
- Read:
  - Dennis M. Ritchie & Ken Thompson, The UNIX Time-Sharing System, Communications of the ACM 17 (1974)
  - Brian W. Kernighan, UNIX: A History and a Memoir (2019)
